concepts.name: Passed pawn

cautions: An outpost that can be neutralised by an equal exchange confers little. Check what can capture the occupant before naming it.
Occupying is not obligatory. The THREAT of occupying can bind the defender while the piece does something else.

concepts.name: Fork
concepts.why: The knight on g3 forks the queen on e4 and the king on f1.
concepts.wording: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.
cautions: A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.

concepts.name: Knight fork
concepts.wording: A knight fork: one knight attacks two or more pieces, and neither interposition nor counter-attack defends, because a knight cannot be blocked and attacks the opposite colour to the one it occupies.
cautions: The landing square must be safe. This base's fork controlled pair shows the same knight move at +7.39 and at +0.57 depending only on whether one bishop guards the square.
A knight fork on a guarded square wins nothing.

concepts.name: Hanging piece
concepts.why: It leaves the queen on e4 hanging — it can simply be taken.
concepts.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Restraint
concepts.wording: Restraint: preventing enemy pawns and pieces from advancing, as progress in its own right. It is the first stage of Nimzowitsch's formula — first restrain, then blockade, finally destroy.
cautions: Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.

concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn
concepts.wording: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.

The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

concepts.name: Blockade

cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concept.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.

concepts.name: Battery
concepts.wording: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
cautions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.

concepts.name: Blockade
concepts.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Material imbalance

concepts.name: Exchange sacrifice
concepts.wording: An exchange sacrifice: rook for a minor piece. First check whether it is forced — if mate or material follows by force, calculate it. If not, name the lasting asset it buys.
cautions: In open positions with files available, a rook is worth more than the nominal margin and the sacrifice is correspondingly worse.
Returning the exchange at the right moment is a standard resource for the defender and must be accounted for.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.wording: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

altConcept.name: Passed pawn
altConcept.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Bad bishop
concepts.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.
